newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore does not rule out more telecom licences.
newsitem.headline: Singapore does not rule out more telecom licences.

text.p: Communications Minister Mah Bow Tan on Wednesday refused to rule out awarding more telecoms licenses after 2002, less than a week after Singapore said it was inviting tenders for commercial phone services from 2002.

"I think this is really a very difficult question to answer. We really do not know what the industry is going to look like after 2002. For me to say now that yes there will be more, or no there won't be is highly academic," Mah told reporters.
Mah declined to estimate how many players he thought Singapore's domestic telecommunications market could sustain.
"That's not really for me to answer," he said after opening the third Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) telecommunication regulators' council meeting.
"The tenderers will have to take a decision as to what the market can bear and they will put in their bids accordingly," he said.
Analysts say two new licences could be up for grabs when the 2002 commercial services bidding battle gets underway.
But they said the domestic market could then find itself trying to sustain up to five players if the one or two licences scheduled to be awarded for a 2000 start are joined by two more in 2002.

Three consortia have qualified to bid for one or two new licences to offer basic public telecommunications services in competition to current monopoly Singapore Telecommunications Ltd from April 1, 2000.
They include a consortium of Cable & Wireless, Hong Kong Telecommunications, Keppel Telecom and Singapore Press Holdings.
A second consortium comprises British Telecommunications, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, Singapore Power and ST Telecommunications.
The third groups SembCorp Ltd, Singapore MRT Ltd and WorldCom Inc.

Mah rejected criticisms that plans announced on Friday by the Telecommunication Authority of Singapore to issue basic telecoms licences for commercial services in Singapore by 2002 created unnecessary uncertainty in the market.

"We reserved the right to open the market for more licences after the year 2000 so this perception in the market place among some people that this is an about turn or a change is unwarranted," Mah said.
Keeping options open over new licences was vital to ensure the most competitive services and up to date technology were available in Singapore, he said.
